critic.argument: The claim rests on a single low-engagement RSS item containing an unsourced assertion with no methodology, no benchmark, no sample, and no corroboration. The actual verifiable content is reportedly just the author's anecdotal observation that ChatGPT and Claude refuse to name public figures while Gemini does not — a self-reported behavioral asymmetry, not a capability finding. 'LLMs can now identify public figures in images' is not even what the evidence supports: the only concrete signal is that one model declined to refuse, which is a policy/guardrail difference, not a demonstrated increase in identification ability. Multimodal models could identify public figures before this item existed, so 'now' implies a temporal capability change that no evidence establishes. The source is also topically peripheral (the cluster's stated topic is AI agents for engineering practice), so the claim is being inflated from a policy-divergence anecdote into a general capability assertion. This is a lexical coincidence between 'LLMs' and 'identify public figures' plus an unverified behavioral report — a thin, uncorroborated, non-measured, non-generalizable data point. It does not survive scrutiny as stated.
